pos: n. (a long-necked migratory bird; used of Hezekiah's chattering in sickness and of the birds that keep their seasons)
etymology: Old English cran. The Hebrew agur is a migratory bird, named in both places beside the swallow; its cry is a harsh repeated note, which is why Hezekiah reached for it.
biblical_def: Hezekiah, given fifteen more years after being told to set his house in order, wrote down what the sickness had been like: “Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me” (Isa 38:14). It is one of the most honest descriptions of extremity in Scripture — not eloquent prayer but the broken repeated noise of a man who cannot form sentences, with his eyes failing from looking up. His conclusion is equally plain: “What shall I say? he hath both spoken unto me, and himself hath done it: I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa 38:15). Jeremiah uses the same bird for a rebuke: “Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; and the turtle and the crane and the swallow observe the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of the LORD” (Jer 8:7). Birds keep an appointment they were never taught. A covenant people, taught for centuries, missed theirs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the crane as a migratory fowl of the genus Ardea, with a long bill, neck and legs, and a loud harsh cry; also a machine for raising weights.
webster_full: CRANE, n. [Sax. cran.] A migratory fowl of the genus Ardea, with a long bill, neck and legs.
The crane has a loud, harsh voice, and flies in flocks at the change of seasons.
Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter. Isa. xxxviii.
2. A machine for raising great weights.
scriptures: Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me.
What shall I say? he hath both spoken unto me, and himself hath done it: I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul.
Jer 8:7
Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; and the turtle and the crane and the swallow observe the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of the LORD.
Mat 6:26
Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?
corruption_summary: Prayer is judged by its fluency, though Isaiah 38 preserves a king's prayer as the chattering of a bird and God answered it.
corruption_paragraphs: Hezekiah's own record of his prayer is a rebuke to every notion that God is moved by well-turned petitions. He chattered like a crane or a swallow; he mourned as a dove; his eyes failed with looking upward; and the whole content of it comes down to five words — O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me. That is the prayer God answered with fifteen years and a sign in the shadow on the dial. Romans says the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered, because we know not what we should pray for as we ought, and Hezekiah's chapter is that verse in narrative form. A believer who cannot pray in sentences is not therefore failing to pray. The corruption to name is not eloquence itself, which is a gift, but the assumption that God hears in proportion to a man's command of language — the very thing the Lord Jesus forbade when He said men are not heard for their much speaking.

Jeremiah's use of the crane sets a different measure. The migratory birds keep their appointed times without instruction, and the prophet's complaint is that a people who had the law, the prophets, the temple and the covenant did not know the judgment of the LORD — that is, they could not read their own season. Every generation of the church has this danger. The stork does not need to be told when to fly; a congregation with Bibles in every hand may still miss what God is doing in its own time and place, because knowing the appointed times requires not information but obedience. Hezekiah, having been spared, said he would go softly all his years, and that phrase is the right posture for anyone who has been brought back from the edge and given time he did not earn.
roots_summary: Hebrew agur (H5693), a crane or migratory bird; with sus (H5483), the swallow, and moed (H4150), an appointed time or season.
roots_lines: Hebrew agur (H5693) — a crane; like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter; Isaiah 38:14, Jeremiah 8:7.
Hebrew tsaphaph (H6850) — to chirp or peep; the sound Hezekiah made in his sickness; Isaiah 38:14.
Hebrew moed (H4150) — an appointed time; the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; Jeremiah 8:7.
Hebrew chasidah (H2624) — the stork, literally the kind or faithful one; Jeremiah 8:7.
Hebrew arab (H6148) — to be surety, to undertake for; undertake for me; Isaiah 38:14.
usage: “Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter” — a king's prayer, described by its owner.
“O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me” — five words, and fifteen years granted.
“My people know not the judgment of the LORD” — birds keep an appointment men missed.

pos: n. (a bird of prey of the hawk kind; named among the fowls held in abomination)
etymology: Old English cyta. The Hebrew ayyah denotes a bird of prey with keen sight, listed in both catalogues of forbidden fowls; the toy kite takes its English name from the bird's hovering flight.
biblical_def: The kite appears in both lists of unclean birds. Leviticus opens the catalogue with a heading that is worth reading whole: “And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray” (Lev 11:13), and then “And the vulture, and the kite after his kind” (Lev 11:14). Deuteronomy has the same birds in a slightly different order: “And the glede, and the kite, and the vulture after his kind” (Deu 14:13). Nearly every fowl on the list is a bird of prey or a carrion eater — creatures that live by blood, or by what is already dead. Israel, a people forbidden to eat blood at all, was not to eat the birds that live on it. The phrase after his kind recurs here as it does throughout the chapter, extending the prohibition to the whole family rather than to a single species, and the chapter's stated purpose governs it all: they were to be holy, for God is holy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the kite as a rapacious fowl of the genus Falco, of the hawk kind, remarkable for gliding through the air without apparent motion of the wings.
webster_full: KITE, n. [Sax. cyta.] A rapacious fowl of the genus Falco, or hawk kind.
It is remarkable for gliding through the air without any apparent motion of its wings.
The vulture, and the kite after his kind. Lev. xi.
2. A light frame of wood and paper, constructed for flying in the air.
scriptures: And the vulture, and the kite after his kind;
And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,
And the glede, and the kite, and the vulture after his kind,

For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
corruption_summary: Small differences between the parallel lists in Leviticus and Deuteronomy are advanced as contradictions, though neither list claims to be exhaustive or ordered.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 give the unclean fowls in slightly different order, and Deuteronomy adds the glede where Leviticus does not. This is regularly listed among the alleged discrepancies of the Pentateuch, usually in support of the theory that the two chapters come from different documentary sources. The observation is real; the inference is not required and the framework behind it is one this dictionary rejects. Deuteronomy is by its own account Moses rehearsing the law to a new generation on the plains of Moab forty years after Sinai, and a rehearsal is not a transcript — a preacher restating his own earlier teaching orders it differently and fills out what needs filling. Neither list is presented as exhaustive; both close with a general clause. The variation is what one expects from the same author addressing a different audience, and it is exactly what the text says is happening.

The character of the list is the more useful observation. Nearly every bird named is a raptor or a scavenger, and Israel was a people to whom the life of the flesh in the blood had been given for atonement upon the altar, and who were therefore forbidden to eat blood at all. Birds that live by blood were placed outside their diet, so that the sanctity of blood was taught in the kitchen as well as at the altar. That is the pattern of the whole law: the great doctrines — life belongs to God, atonement is by blood, this people is separated — are pressed into the ordinary furniture of a life until they cannot be forgotten. The doctrine outlives the diet, and the New Testament keeps it: ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, but with the precious blood of Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew ayyah (H344), a kite or bird of prey; with daah (H1676), the glede or vulture of Deuteronomy 14:13, and sheqets (H8263), an abomination.
roots_lines: Hebrew ayyah (H344) — a kite, a hawk-like bird of keen sight; Leviticus 11:14, Job 28:7.
Hebrew daah (H1676) — a bird of prey, rendered vulture and glede; Deuteronomy 14:13.
Hebrew min (H4327) — kind; after his kind, extending the prohibition to the family; Leviticus 11:14.
Hebrew sheqets (H8263) — an abomination, a detestable thing; the heading of the whole list; Leviticus 11:13.
Hebrew dam (H1818) — blood; the life of the flesh, given upon the altar to make atonement; Leviticus 17:11.
usage: “The vulture, and the kite after his kind” — the prohibition covers the family.
“Ye shall have in abomination among the fowls” — the heading over the list.
“The glede, and the kite, and the vulture” — the same law, rehearsed in Moab.

pos: n. (an unclean fowl of the law; the Authorized Version's older spelling of cuckoo, though the bird intended is uncertain)
etymology: From the bird's call, Old French cucu; the 1611 spelling cuckow preserves the older English form. The Hebrew shachaph may name a gull or a shearwater rather than a cuckoo.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice, in the parallel lists of forbidden fowls: “And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind” (Lev 11:16), and identically in the rehearsal of the law (Deu 14:15). Nothing else in Scripture is said about it, and the identification is not certain; the Hebrew word suggests a lean or slender bird and has been rendered gull or sea-mew as well as cuckoo. What the verse does establish is the shape of the whole catalogue: a run of night birds and hunters, each named, each with its family included by the phrase after his kind. Leviticus adds the wider rule about winged creatures: “All fowls that creep, going upon all four, shall be an abomination unto you” (Lev 11:20). And the chapter's purpose remains what it states at its close — a people sanctified because their God is holy (Lev 11:44).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the cuckoo as a bird of the genus Cuculus, named from the sound of its note, and notorious for laying its eggs in the nests of other birds.
webster_full: CUCKOO, n. [from the sound of its note.] A bird of the genus Cuculus.
The European cuckoo lays its eggs in the nests of other birds, to be hatched and reared by them.
The owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow. Lev. xi.
CUCKOO-FLOWER, n. A plant, a species of Cardamine.
scriptures: And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,
And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,
All fowls that creep, going upon all four, shall be an abomination unto you.

For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
corruption_summary: An archaic spelling and an uncertain bird are treated as evidence that the Authorized Version is unreliable, when the difficulty is lexical and is shared by every translation.
corruption_paragraphs: Cuckow is the 1611 spelling of a word we now write cuckoo, and the bird behind the Hebrew shachaph is genuinely uncertain — modern versions render it gull, sea gull, or long-eared owl, and none of them can be sure either. Two conclusions are drawn too quickly from this. The first is that the Authorized Version is obsolete because its English has aged; but an old spelling is not an error, and a reader who learns a hundred such words has gained access to the most influential English book ever printed rather than lost anything. The second is that uncertainty about a bird undermines confidence in Scripture; it does not, because the doctrine of the passage does not rest on the species. Every translation faces the same lexical gap, and honesty about it is a mark of careful work rather than a crack in the foundation.

It is worth saying plainly what this dictionary holds, since these lists are where the question usually surfaces. The Authorized Version is our working English text and its accuracy in the things that matter is not in doubt; where a Hebrew term for a bird or a stone cannot now be identified, that is a limit of our knowledge and not a defect in the word God gave. The standard the dictionary applies to itself is stricter than the one usually applied to translations: a quotation must match the version it claims, word for word. What ruins credibility is not an archaic spelling but a modern rendering printed under a label it does not belong to — and that is a fault of quotation, not of translation.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachaph (H7828), an unclean fowl rendered cuckow; from a root suggesting leanness; with tachmas (H8464), the night hawk, and netz (H5322), the hawk.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachaph (H7828) — rendered cuckow; occurring only in the two lists; Leviticus 11:16, Deuteronomy 14:15.
Hebrew tachmas (H8464) — the night hawk; named immediately before it; Leviticus 11:16.
Hebrew netz (H5322) — a hawk; the hawk after his kind; Leviticus 11:16, Job 39:26.
Hebrew bath yaanah — the owl, literally daughter of greed or of the wilderness; Leviticus 11:16.
Hebrew oph (H5775) — a fowl, anything that flies; the general category; Leviticus 11:13.
usage: “The owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow” — a run of night birds, each named.
“After his kind” — the family included with the bird.
“All fowls that creep, going upon all four” — the wider rule of the chapter.

pos: n. (an unclean fowl of the law; the Hebrew probably names an ibis or water hen rather than the swan)
etymology: Old English swan. The Hebrew tinshemeth is from a root meaning to breathe or pant, and the same word is rendered mole among the creeping things — so the translators used two English names for one Hebrew word in two contexts.
biblical_def: Twice in the lists: “And the swan, and the pelican, and the gier eagle” (Lev 11:18), and “The little owl, and the great owl, and the swan” (Deu 14:16). The Hebrew word behind it, tinshemeth, is the same one rendered mole at Leviticus 11:30, which tells the reader something useful about how the Authorized Version works: where a Hebrew term names an animal no longer identifiable, the translators supplied a familiar English creature that fitted the context, a bird among birds and a creeper among creepers. Many now take the word to mean the ibis or a water hen. The verse's force does not depend on it. What the two lists do is fence a people about with distinctions they could not escape at any meal, so that holiness was not an idea kept for the sanctuary. The chapter says so in as many words: ye shall be holy; for I am holy (Lev 11:44).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the swan as a large aquatic fowl of the genus Anas, with a long neck, noted for its white plumage and graceful motion on the water.
webster_full: SWAN, n. [Sax. swan.] A large aquatic fowl of the genus Anas.
The neck is very long, the plumage generally white, and the bird moves on the water with great grace.
And the swan, and the pelican, and the gier eagle. Lev. xi.
SWAN-SKIN, n. A species of soft flannel.
scriptures: And the swan, and the pelican, and the gier eagle,
The little owl, and the great owl, and the swan,
And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,

For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
corruption_summary: Holiness is thought of as an inward disposition only, while Leviticus 11 attaches it to a table, a pot, an oven and a list of birds.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's holiness reaches into the material furniture of a life. Leviticus 11 is not a chapter of abstractions; it regulates what may be eaten, what may be touched, which pots must be broken, which ovens must be pulled down, and how long a defilement lasts. And it grounds all of it in the character of God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy. The ceremonial particulars are fulfilled in Christ and are not binding now; what is not fulfilled and never expires is the principle that the God who is holy claims the ordinary. Paul makes the same move for the church when he says whether ye eat or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.

There is a second, quieter lesson in the fact that one Hebrew word became swan in one verse and mole in another. Translation involves judgment, and honest translators say so. The Authorized Version's own translators wrote in their preface that variety in rendering was deliberate and that they had not tied themselves to an identity of phrasing. That is a different thing altogether from what a modern reader must actually guard against, which is a quotation printed under a version's name that does not match that version's words. A translator's judgment is public and reviewable; a misattributed quotation is not. The remedy in both cases is the same: go to the text, and check.
roots_summary: Hebrew tinshemeth (H8580), rendered swan among the fowls and mole among the creeping things; from nasham, to breathe or pant.
roots_lines: Hebrew tinshemeth (H8580) — rendered swan in the bird lists and mole among the creepers; Leviticus 11:18, Leviticus 11:30.
Hebrew qaath (H6893) — the pelican; named beside it; Leviticus 11:18, Psalm 102:6.
Hebrew racham (H7360) — the gier eagle; the third bird of the verse; Leviticus 11:18.
Hebrew kos (H3563) — the little owl; Deuteronomy 14:16.
Hebrew qadosh (H6918) — holy; for I am holy, the ground of the entire chapter; Leviticus 11:44.
usage: “And the swan, and the pelican, and the gier eagle” — three unclean fowls in one line.
One Hebrew word, two English names — swan among birds, mole among creepers.
“Ye shall be holy; for I am holy” — holiness attached to a table.

pos: n. (an unclean fowl of the law, written night hawk in the Authorized Version; a bird of the darkness)
etymology: English night with hawk. The Hebrew tachmas comes from a root meaning violence or robbery, so the bird is named for its manner of taking rather than for its shape.
biblical_def: The bird appears twice, in the parallel catalogues: “And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind” (Lev 11:16), and the same words in the rehearsal of the law (Deu 14:15). It stands in a run of night birds — owls before it, and the hawk after — and its Hebrew name is built on the word for violence. That is characteristic of the list as a whole: the fowls held in abomination are, with few exceptions, birds that hunt or scavenge, and the heading is uncompromising: “And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination” (Lev 11:13). Nothing in the law suggests these creatures are evil in themselves — God feeds the young ravens which cry, and the Lord Jesus told men to behold the fowls of the air, for the heavenly Father feedeth them (Mat 6:26). They were simply set outside the boundary of a people's table for a season, that the boundary might be felt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives the night-hawk as a fowl that flies and feeds by night, of the goatsucker kind; a bird of dusk and darkness rather than of the day.
webster_full: NIGHT-HAWK, n. A fowl of the goatsucker kind, that flies and takes its prey in the evening and night.
The owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow. Lev. xi.
NIGHT-BIRD, n. A bird that flies only at night.
NIGHT, n. That part of the natural day when the sun is beneath the horizon.
scriptures: And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,
And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,
And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,
Mat 6:26
Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?
corruption_summary: Creatures declared unclean are read as creatures declared evil, which flatly contradicts the God who made them and feeds them.
corruption_paragraphs: The word abomination in Leviticus 11:13 is strong and it is regularly misapplied. It does not mean that the eagle, the ospray or the night hawk is wicked, or that God dislikes what He made. Genesis says He made every winged fowl after his kind and saw that it was good, and Psalm 147 says He gives to the beast his food, and to the young ravens which cry — the raven being on this same forbidden list. The term marks a ritual boundary for one nation for one era: these are not to be eaten by you. Reading a ceremonial classification as a moral one has produced a great deal of bad theology, including the notion that matter itself is dirty, which is the ancient error of the Gnostics and stands against a Bible whose God took flesh and rose in a body.

The New Testament settles the status of the creatures directly and Christians should be clear about it. Peter was shown a sheet of all manner of fourfooted beasts and creeping things and fowls of the air and told to rise, kill, and eat; when he objected that he had never eaten anything common or unclean, the voice answered, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. Mark says of the Lord's teaching on defilement that He purged all meats. Paul writes that every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. The boundary has been moved from the plate to the heart, where the Lord Himself located defilement: not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man, but that which cometh out of the mouth, for out of the heart proceed evil thoughts.
roots_summary: Hebrew tachmas (H8464), the night hawk; from chamas, violence; with sheqets (H8263), abomination, and koinos (G2839), common, in Peter's vision.
roots_lines: Hebrew tachmas (H8464) — the night hawk; built on the root for violence or robbery; Leviticus 11:16, Deuteronomy 14:15.
Hebrew chamas (H2555) — violence; the earth was filled with violence before the flood; Genesis 6:11.
Hebrew sheqets (H8263) — an abomination, a ritually detestable thing; Leviticus 11:13.
Greek koinos (G2839) — common, ceremonially unclean; what God hath cleansed, call not thou common; Acts 10:15.
Greek katharizo (G2511) — to cleanse; saying this, he purged all meats; Mark 7:19.
usage: “The owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow” — the birds of the dark.
“They shall not be eaten, they are an abomination” — a boundary, not a verdict on the creature.
“Your heavenly Father feedeth them” — said of the same fowls.

pos: n. (the great flightless bird of the desert; in Job an example of a creature God made without wisdom on purpose)
etymology: Old French ostruce, from Latin avis struthio, the struthious bird. The Hebrew phrase in Job 39 is renanim, the wailing or shrill ones, named for the bird's cry in the night.
biblical_def: God's own speech out of the whirlwind puts the ostrich before Job as a question: “Gavest thou the goodly wings unto the peacocks? or wings and feathers unto the ostrich?” (Job 39:13). What follows is one of the strangest passages in Scripture. “Which leaveth her eggs in the earth, and warmeth them in dust” (Job 39:14) — the bird is described as careless toward her young, hardened against them as though they were not hers. And then the explanation, which is the point of the whole section: “Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding” (Job 39:17). The deficiency is not an accident and not a fall; God made her so, and says so, and in the next breath describes her scorning the horse and his rider when she lifts herself to run. A creature at once foolish and magnificent, made deliberately in that shape, is set before a man demanding that God explain Himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the ostrich as the largest of fowls, of the genus Struthio, with wings unfit for flight but great swiftness of foot, inhabiting the deserts of Africa and Arabia.
webster_full: OSTRICH, n. [L. avis struthio.] A fowl constituting the genus Struthio, the largest of the feathered tribe.
The wings are short and unfit for flight, but the bird runs with great swiftness.
Wings and feathers unto the ostrich. Job xxxix.
It inhabits the sandy deserts of Africa and Arabia.
scriptures: Gavest thou the goodly wings unto the peacocks? or wings and feathers unto the ostrich?
Which leaveth her eggs in the earth, and warmeth them in dust,
Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding.
And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.
corruption_summary: God is expected to justify the design of the world at the bar of human sense, and Job 39 answers a suffering man with a foolish bird God made on purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: The problem of suffering is usually posed as a demand for explanation, and Job's friends had already supplied several bad ones. When God finally speaks, He offers none. He asks about the foundations of the earth, the springs of the sea, the wild ass, the unicorn, the war horse, the hawk and the ostrich — four chapters of questions about creatures, and not one sentence about Job's losses. The ostrich is the sharpest of them, because God volunteers that He made her without wisdom. The world contains a bird that abandons her eggs in the sand, and God says plainly that this is His doing and not a defect that slipped past Him. A theology which requires every feature of creation to be justifiable to human judgment cannot survive Job 39, and the book is in the canon partly to make sure it does not.

What that does for a sufferer is easily mistaken for cruelty and is in fact the only comfort available. Job does not receive an account of the wager in heaven; the reader has it and Job never does. What he receives is God, speaking, at length, about a world so vast and so strange that his framework for judging it is exposed as too small. And his answer is not resentment: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth thee; wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes. That is the resolution the book offers, and Job 28 had already stated where wisdom is actually found and where it is not: not in the deep, not in the sea, not in the path the vulture's eye has not seen — but, behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom.
roots_summary: Hebrew renanim (H7443), the shrill or wailing ones, rendered ostrich in Job 39:13; bath yaanah, the ostrich elsewhere; with chokmah (H2451), wisdom.
roots_lines: Hebrew renanim (H7443) — the wailing ones, rendered ostrich; named for the cry, not the shape; Job 39:13.
Hebrew bath yaanah — the ostrich, literally daughter of the wilderness; Isaiah 13:21, Micah 1:8.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; God hath deprived her of wisdom; Job 39:17.
Hebrew binah (H998) — understanding; neither hath he imparted to her understanding; Job 39:17.
Hebrew yirath adonai — the fear of the Lord; that is wisdom, and to depart from evil is understanding; Job 28:28.
usage: “Wings and feathers unto the ostrich” — a question, not an explanation.
“God hath deprived her of wisdom” — volunteered by God about His own work.
“The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom” — where the book says it is found.

pos: n. (a ground-nesting game bird; hunted in the mountains, and the figure of a man who gathers riches wrongly)
etymology: Old French pertriz, from Latin perdix. The Hebrew qore means the caller, named from its cry; it nests on the ground and is hunted on foot through the hills.
biblical_def: David uses the bird of himself: “Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains” (1Sa 26:20). Partridge hunting in that country was done by pursuit — driving the bird until it could not fly again — and David is saying that a king with an army is wearing out one man through the hills. Jeremiah uses it for the ruin of dishonest gain: “As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool” (Jer 17:11). The bird broods a clutch that never hatches, and the man broods a fortune that never becomes his. Three things are asserted: the riches will be left, the leaving will be premature, and the verdict on the man is fool — the same word the Lord Jesus used of the rich man who pulled down his barns.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the partridge as a wild fowl of the genus Tetrao, esteemed for food, which nests on the ground and is much hunted.
webster_full: PARTRIDGE, n. [L. perdix.] A wild fowl of the genus Tetrao, much esteemed for food.
The partridge builds its nest on the ground, and is hunted with dogs.
As when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains. 1 Sam. xxvi.
PARTRIDGE-BERRY, n. A plant, a species of Gaultheria.
scriptures: Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains.
As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool.
After whom is the king of Israel come out? after whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea.
There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise:
corruption_summary: Wealth is judged by amount and not by method, while Jeremiah 17:11 makes the manner of getting the whole issue and calls the successful getter a fool.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah's proverb turns on four words: and not by right. He is not describing a poor investment or a market reversal; the man succeeds in getting the riches, and the getting is crooked. What follows is not a moral about greed in general but three specific claims. He shall leave them — the transfer is certain. In the midst of his days — the leaving is early, before the enjoyment. And at his end he shall be a fool — the final assessment is not that he was clever and unlucky but that he was stupid, which is exactly the Lord's verdict on the man with the barns: Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee. Our own age evaluates a fortune almost entirely by its size and its legality, and the prophets evaluate it by whether it was got by right and what it did to the man who got it.

David's use of the bird is the gentler and the more personal. Hunting a partridge in the mountains meant following it up the slopes until it was too spent to rise, and that is what Saul's campaign amounted to — a national army wearing down one man who had done him no wrong and had twice spared his life. David's appeal is not to Saul's conscience alone but to God's presence: let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD. He is asking the LORD to notice, which is what a man does when there is no other court. And the LORD did notice; Saul died on Gilboa and David wept for him. A believer hunted in the same way is not without recourse; he has the same appeal, and the same Judge.
roots_summary: Hebrew qore (H7124), the partridge, literally the caller; with osher (H6239), riches, and nabal (H5036), a fool — Jeremiah's last word on the man.
roots_lines: Hebrew qore (H7124) — a partridge, the caller; hunted in the mountains; 1 Samuel 26:20, Jeremiah 17:11.
Hebrew osher (H6239) — riches; he that getteth riches, and not by right; Jeremiah 17:11.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, right; not by right is the hinge of the proverb; Jeremiah 17:11.
Hebrew nabal (H5036) — a fool, a vile man; at his end shall be a fool; Jeremiah 17:11.
Greek aphron (G878) — senseless, foolish; Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee; Luke 12:20.
usage: “As when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains” — a bird driven until it cannot rise.
“As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not” — a fortune brooded and never hatched.
“At his end shall be a fool” — the verdict on a successful getter.

pos: n. (a flying creature of the night, listed with the unclean fowls; and, with the mole, the recipient of cast-away idols)
etymology: Middle English bakke, from a Scandinavian root. The Hebrew atalleph names the bat, which the law classes among the fowls because it flies, according to the ordinary way people speak rather than a modern taxonomy.
biblical_def: The bat closes both lists of unclean fowls: “And the stork, the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat” (Lev 11:19), and identically at Deuteronomy 14:18. It is the last name in a long catalogue, and the only creature in it that is not a bird. Isaiah gives it its great appearance: “In that day a man shall cast his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which they made each one for himself to worship, to the moles and to the bats” (Isa 2:20). Bats live in caves and ruined places, and the same chapter says men will go into the clefts of the rocks and into the tops of the ragged rocks for fear of the LORD; so the idols are flung into the very holes their owners are running toward. Isaiah elsewhere fills a judged land with such creatures — “the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it” (Isa 34:11). The birds of the dark inherit what proud men leave behind.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the bat as a quadruped of the genus Vespertilio, with wings formed of a membrane, which flies in the evening and lodges in caves and ruins.
webster_full: BAT, n. An animal of the genus Vespertilio, having wings of membrane extended between the toes.
It flies in the twilight and night, and lodges by day in caverns and old buildings.
The lapwing, and the bat. Lev. xi.
BAT, n. A heavy stick or club; a piece of wood with one end thicker than the other.
scriptures: And the stork, the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat.
And the stork, and the heron after her kind, and the lapwing, and the bat.
Isa 2:20
In that day a man shall cast his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which they made each one for himself to worship, to the moles and to the bats;
But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness.
corruption_summary: That Leviticus classes the bat with fowls is offered as proof of biblical error, though the text is using ordinary speech about flying creatures, not a modern taxonomy.
corruption_paragraphs: The bat is a standing exhibit in the argument that the Bible contains scientific mistakes: it is a mammal, and Leviticus lists it among the fowls. The objection assumes that the chapter is offering a classification of the animal kingdom by descent and physiology, which is a category invented in the eighteenth century and later. The Hebrew word rendered fowl is oph, from a root meaning to fly, and it means simply the flying things — a functional grouping, exactly as an English speaker still calls a whale a sea creature or speaks of the sun rising. Leviticus 11:20 makes the same functional move with insects, speaking of fowls that creep, going upon all four. Scripture is inerrant in what it asserts, and it asserts here which creatures Israel may eat, in the ordinary language of the people who had to obey it.

Isaiah's use of the bat is where the entry earns its keep. The idols of silver and gold were made each one for himself to worship — commissioned, paid for, and known to be manufactured — and in the day of the LORD's terror they are thrown to the bats and moles while their owners scramble into the rocks. That is not a picture of men repenting; it is a picture of men discarding. There is a moment, and Scripture insists it is coming, when every substitute for God is instantly and universally seen to be worthless, and the seeing will not save anybody who waited for it. The gospel calls men to make the same judgment now, while it can be made with a whole heart: turn from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven.
roots_summary: Hebrew atalleph (H5847), a bat; with oph (H5775), a flying thing, the functional category of the list, and elil (H457), an idol.
roots_lines: Hebrew atalleph (H5847) — a bat; last named in both lists of unclean fowls; Leviticus 11:19, Deuteronomy 14:18.
Hebrew oph (H5775) — a flying creature, from uph, to fly; the functional category rendered fowl.
Hebrew chapharperah (H2661) — a mole, a digger; named with the bat as recipient of the idols; Isaiah 2:20.
Hebrew elil (H457) — an idol, a thing of nought; Isaiah 2:20, Psalm 96:5.
Hebrew tohu (H8414) — confusion, emptiness; the line of confusion stretched over a judged land; Isaiah 34:11.
usage: “The lapwing, and the bat” — last in the list, and the only one that is not a bird.
“To the moles and to the bats” — silver gods thrown into the dark.
“The owl also and the raven shall dwell in it” — who inherits what pride leaves.

pos: n. (a carrion bird of the unclean list; and in Job the possessor of the keenest eye in creation, which still cannot find wisdom)
etymology: Latin vultur. The Hebrew daah and dayyah name birds of prey; ayyah at Job 28:7 is rendered vulture, and the passage turns entirely on the sharpness of the creature's sight.
biblical_def: In the law: “And the vulture, and the kite after his kind” (Lev 11:14), and in the rehearsal, “And the glede, and the kite, and the vulture after his kind” (Deu 14:13), among the fowls Israel was to have in abomination (Lev 11:13). But the great use is in Job's hymn to wisdom. Chapter 28 describes men mining — sinking shafts, cutting rivers among the rocks, bringing to light things hid — and then says of the way to wisdom: “There is a path which no fowl knoweth, and which the vulture's eye hath not seen” (Job 28:7). The vulture is the proverbial far-seer, and its eye has not found this road. The chapter presses the question — “But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?” (Job 28:12) — through the deep and the sea and the price of gold, and answers it at last from outside the search altogether: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the vulture as a rapacious fowl of the genus Vultur, which feeds chiefly on carrion, remarkable for its keenness of sight and smell.
webster_full: VULTURE, n. [L. vultur.] A genus of rapacious fowls.
The vulture feeds chiefly on carrion, and is remarkable for the acuteness of its sight and smell.
Which the vulture's eye hath not seen. Job xxviii.
VULTURINE, a. Belonging to a vulture; rapacious.
scriptures: Job 28:7
There is a path which no fowl knoweth, and which the vulture's eye hath not seen:
But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?
And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.
And the vulture, and the kite after his kind;
corruption_summary: Wisdom is sought as information to be discovered, and Job 28 says the sharpest eye in creation has not found the path and that God gave the answer by speaking.
corruption_paragraphs: Job 28 is the most sustained argument in Scripture about the limits of investigation, and it is not hostile to investigation at all. The chapter opens by admiring it: men have a vein for silver and a place for gold, they put an end to darkness, they cut out rivers among the rocks, and the earth's hidden things are brought to light. What it denies is that the same method reaches wisdom. The path is one no fowl knows and the vulture's eye has not seen; the deep says it is not in me, the sea says it is not with me; it cannot be gotten for gold, nor valued with the precious onyx. That is a direct contradiction of the working assumption of a scientific age, which is that everything worth knowing is in principle findable by search. Some things are found only because they are told, and the chapter ends with God telling.

The answer, when it comes, is startling for its plainness after twenty-seven verses of unreachable places: Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding. Wisdom turns out not to be an elite attainment but a stance available to any man, and it has two parts, one Godward and one moral. The vulture's eye is superb and useless here; a farmer in the fear of God has what the bird cannot see. That is also why the New Testament locates wisdom in a Person — Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and who is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. The path was never going to be spotted from the air. It had to be revealed, and it was.
roots_summary: Hebrew ayyah (H344), rendered vulture at Job 28:7; daah (H1676) and dayyah (H1772) in the law; with chokmah (H2451), wisdom.
roots_lines: Hebrew ayyah (H344) — a bird of prey of keen sight; which the vulture's eye hath not seen; Job 28:7.
Hebrew daah (H1676) — a bird of prey, rendered vulture; Leviticus 11:14.
Hebrew nathib (H5410) — a path, a beaten track; there is a path which no fowl knoweth; Job 28:7.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; where shall wisdom be found; Job 28:12.
Hebrew yirah (H3374) — fear, reverence; the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; Job 28:28.
usage: “Which the vulture's eye hath not seen” — the sharpest sight in creation, and it misses the road.
“Where shall wisdom be found?” — asked after the deep and the sea have both answered no.
“The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom” — told, because it could not be found.

pos: n. pl. (rock badgers of the cliffs; a feeble folk that build in the rocks, and one of the four little wise things)
etymology: Middle English coni, from Latin cuniculus, a rabbit — the older English name for the rabbit. The Hebrew shaphan is the rock hyrax of the Palestinian cliffs, a small hoofed animal with no defence but its shelter.
biblical_def: Twice the word appears, and both times it is about where the creature lives. The psalmist, cataloguing God's ordering of creation: “The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies” (Psa 104:18) — every creature has been given a place suited to it, which is the psalm's whole argument for providence. And Agur, in his four small wonders: “The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks” (Pro 30:26), one of the “four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise” (Pro 30:24). The animal has no speed, no size, no weapons; its entire wisdom is knowing where to live. Agur does not commend it for overcoming its weakness but for accepting it and building accordingly. The Rock in Scripture is a name of God from Moses' song onward, and a feeble folk that makes its house in the rock is as good a picture of the church as the Old Testament provides.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the coney as a rabbit; and notes the Scripture coney as an animal of the rocks in Palestine, feeble but wise in its habitation.
webster_full: CONEY, n. A rabbit; a quadruped of the genus Lepus.
The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks. Prov. xxx.
The animal of Scripture so called is supposed to be the hyrax of the rocks of Syria.
CONEY-BURROW, n. A place where rabbits burrow in the earth.
scriptures: The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies.
The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks;
There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise:
These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,
corruption_summary: Weakness is treated as a problem to be overcome by effort, while Proverbs 30:26 commends a feeble creature precisely for building where its weakness is answered.
corruption_paragraphs: Agur's four small things are wise in different ways — the ants prepare, the locusts keep order, the spider takes hold — and the conies are wise in the least heroic way of all: they know they are feeble and they live in the rocks. There is no suggestion that the creature improves, trains, or compensates. Its wisdom consists entirely in choosing a dwelling that makes its weakness irrelevant. That runs against the whole temper of self-improvement, in its secular form and in its religious one, where a Christian is exhorted to overcome his weakness by discipline and is left ashamed when it persists. Paul was given a thorn that did not leave, and was told, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. His conclusion was not to become strong but to take pleasure in infirmities, that the power of Christ might rest upon him.

The rock is the other half of the lesson and it is not an accident of habitat. He is the Rock, his work is perfect, says the song of Moses; the LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer, says David; and Paul says of the wilderness rock that followed Israel, and that Rock was Christ. A feeble folk making their houses in the rocks is therefore a picture with a name attached. The church is not commended in Scripture for its resources; Paul says not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble are called, and gives the reason — that no flesh should glory in his presence. Psalm 104 completes the thought by insisting the arrangement is God's doing: He appointed the high hills for the wild goats and the rocks for the conies, and He has provided a refuge suited to exactly what His people are.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaphan (H8227), the coney or rock badger; with sela (H5553), a cliff or rock, and tsur (H6697), the Rock, a name of God.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaphan (H8227) — the coney, the rock hyrax; the rocks for the conies; Psalm 104:18, Proverbs 30:26.
Hebrew sela (H5553) — a cliff, a crag; where they make their houses; Proverbs 30:26.
Hebrew tsur (H6697) — a rock; He is the Rock, his work is perfect; Deuteronomy 32:4.
Hebrew machaseh (H4268) — a refuge; the high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; Psalm 104:18.
Greek astheneia (G769) — weakness, infirmity; my strength is made perfect in weakness; 2 Corinthians 12:9.
usage: “The rocks for the conies” — a place appointed to a creature.
“A feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks” — wisdom that does not deny weakness.
“Little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise” — Agur's standard for greatness.
